draft.title: Peacekeeping
card: UN peacekeeping sends international personnel, such as soldiers, police and civilian staff, to help keep peace in places affected by conflict. Missions are usually set up by the Security Council.
Peacekeepers normally work with the consent of the parties to the conflict. They are there to support a peace, not to fight one side.
Their tasks can include monitoring ceasefires, protecting civilians, helping with elections and supporting local police and government.
Timor-Leste is an example. After the 1999 violence around its vote on independence, UN missions helped keep order and rebuild the country. Australia took a large part in these efforts.
draft.remember: Peacekeepers support a peace that the parties have agreed to. They do not join the fighting.

a.q: Why do UN peacekeepers normally need the consent of the parties to a conflict?
opts: They are there to support a peace, not to fight a side
They are paid for by the groups they are sent to watch
They can only be sent to countries that are UN members
They must wait for each party to approve every action
a.why: Peacekeepers work to support a peace that the parties have accepted, so consent is the normal basis for a mission. It is not about who pays or who belongs to the UN, and the card does not say every action needs approval.
a.clue: Think about what peacekeepers are there to do, and what they are not there to do.

b.q: After a ceasefire between two armed groups in a fictional country, Varnia, the Security Council sets up a mission. Which task fits UN peacekeeping best?
opts: Monitoring the ceasefire and helping protect civilians
Fighting one group to force it to give up its weapons
Taking over the government of Varnia until a vote is held
Trying leaders of both groups for crimes in Varnia
b.why: Monitoring a ceasefire and protecting civilians are tasks the card lists for peacekeepers. Fighting one side goes against supporting a peace the parties agreed to. Running the government and trying leaders are not tasks the card gives to peacekeepers.
b.clue: Which task supports an agreed peace instead of taking a side?

a.best: They are there to support a peace, not to fight a side

b.best: Monitoring the ceasefire and helping protect civilians

problems.detail: The remember line says peacekeepers support a peace the parties 'have agreed to' and 'do not join the fighting', with no qualifier. The card says they 'normally' work with consent and are 'not to fight one side'. Peacekeepers can use force in self-defence or to protect civilians, so the line is more absolute than the card.

The distractor 'Taking over the government of Varnia until a vote is held' is presented, and explained in the why, as something peacekeeping does not do. In the card's own example, the UN Transitional Administration in East Timor (UNTAET, 1999 to 2002) did govern Timor-Leste until independence. Monitoring is still the best answer, but students who know the Timor-Leste case could be misled. Consider replacing this distractor.

check.summary: The answers are sound, but the remember line is more absolute than the card ('do not join the fighting', with consent dropping 'normally'). One distractor in question b, running the government until a vote, is something the UN actually did in the card's own Timor-Leste example.

proposal.title: Peacekeeping
card: UN peacekeeping sends international personnel, such as soldiers, police and civilian staff, to help keep peace in places affected by conflict. Missions are usually set up by the Security Council.
Peacekeepers normally work with the consent of the parties to the conflict. They are there to support a peace, not to fight one side or help one side win.

Peacekeepers may use force in self-defence and, under some missions, to protect civilians. Their tasks can include monitoring ceasefires, protecting civilians, helping with elections and supporting local police and government.
Timor-Leste is an example. After the 1999 violence around its vote on independence, UN missions helped keep order and rebuild the country. Australia took a large part in these efforts.
proposal.remember: Peacekeepers usually work with consent and support a peace without taking sides. They may use force, such as in self-defence.

a.q: Which statement best describes how UN peacekeepers usually work?
opts: With consent, supporting peace without taking a side
Without consent, defeating the side that broke the peace
With consent, but never using force, even in self-defence
Without consent, judging which side was in the right
a.why: Peacekeepers normally have the parties' consent and support a peace without taking sides. The tempting option about never using force is wrong, because peacekeepers may use force in self-defence and sometimes to protect civilians.
a.clue: Think about consent, sides and when force may be used.

b.q: After a ceasefire between two armed groups in a fictional country, Varnia, the Security Council sets up a mission. Which task fits UN peacekeeping best?
opts: Monitoring the ceasefire and helping protect civilians
Fighting one group to force it to give up its weapons
Helping the stronger group win the coming election
Arming one group so it can defend its own territory
b.why: Monitoring a ceasefire and protecting civilians are tasks peacekeepers can carry out while staying impartial. Arming one group may sound defensive, but it still helps one side, which goes against supporting a peace without taking sides.
b.clue: Which task supports the peace without favouring either group?

a.best: With consent, supporting peace without taking a side

b.best: Monitoring the ceasefire and helping protect civilians
